docs.title: Refab Artist
docs.text:
Turn a 3D model into flat parts you can cut,with steps to put them back together.

Download for Mac Read the guide

For Apple silicon Macs running macOS 15 or later. Free and open source (GPL-3.0).

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Refab Artist is a Mac app for makers who build objects from sheet material. Open a 3D model, choose how you want to build it, tell the app what you are cutting from (plywood, MDF, acrylic, card), and it works out the flat parts, lays them out on your sheets, and numbers them. You export the sheets for your laser cutter or CNC router, or print them and cut by hand. The assembly steps then walk you through putting the parts together.

It also has a set of tools for 3D printing and casting: splitting a model into printable pieces, making casting molds, adding lattices and supports, and repairing broken meshes.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Makers with a laser cutter, a CNC router, a craft cutter or a good knife, who want to turn a sculpt or a scan into a physical object made of layers, ribs or folded card.
  • Makerspaces, classrooms and small fab shops.
  • People who 3D print and cast their own work and want help splitting, moulding and repairing models.

You do not need to know CAD. You do need a 3D model in STL or OBJ format.

docs.title: What each mode makes
docs.text: These pictures are drawn from the files Refab Artist exports, using the project's own test models. They are illustrations of the output, not screenshots of the app window.

docs.title: Stacked
docs.text: Parallel layers along one axis. Cut them out, glue them up in order, and the model appears as a terraced solid. More

docs.title: Interlocked
docs.text: Two families of slices with half-lap slots where they cross, so the parts slide together into a grid. More

docs.title: Radial
docs.text: Rings stacked up the model and fins fanned around its centre, notched together. More

docs.title: Curve
docs.text: One family of slices crossed by ribs that follow a curve you shape. More

docs.title: Folded
docs.text: The surface unfolded into flat nets with fold lines and joinery. Cut, fold and join. Best for card and thin sheet. More

docs.title: 3D Slices
docs.text: A layered mesh for 3D printing: layers that keep the model's real surface. More

docs.title: Structures
docs.text: Lattice and pattern infill, supports, and strut skins, as printable meshes. More

docs.title: Partition
docs.text: Split a model into watertight pieces that fit your printer, with locating keys at every seam, or into pieces that can be moulded. More

docs.title: MotherMold
docs.text: A 3D-printable casting mold around your model, in keyed parts with a clamping rim, a pour hole and vents. More

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
  • macOS 15 (Sequoia) or newer. Version 0.1.0 was built and checked on macOS 26.
  • A 3D model as an STL or OBJ file.
  • Sheet material and a way to cut it, for the cut-sheet modes. A 3D printer, for the mesh modes.

Install Refab Artist Getting started

Version 0.1.0 is the first release

The checks run before each release show that exported files are consistent and cuttable. No parts have been cut and assembled in real material for this release, so cut a small test piece first. Cutting and fit shows how.

docs.title: 3D Slices
docs.text:
3D Slices cuts the model into contiguous layers along one axis, and each layer keeps the model's real 3D surface on its side walls. Stack the layers and you rebuild the model as peel-apart bands. The result is a printable layered mesh. There is no flat cut sheet.

It is Stacked with true side walls: Stacked extrudes each cross-section straight up into a flat plate, while 3D Slices keeps the surface between the cuts.

A layered mesh of an organic blob, in bands about 4 mm deep.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You want to 3D print a model in layers that can be separated, painted or assembled one band at a time.
  • You want a layered look in print without cutting sheet material.

For flat parts you cut from sheet, use Stacked.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Slice depth (0.5 to 100 mm, 10 to start with): the spacing between layers.
  • Distribute count (1 to 240): turn it on to choose an even number of layers instead; this overrides and greys out Slice depth.
  • Slice Direction: tilt the cut away from vertical.

3D Slices builds a mesh, so it has no Manufacturing Settings: stock, slots and sheets do not change it, and the section is not shown.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• STL or OBJ only. The layers tile the whole model with no gaps; the model's own top and bottom surfaces close the first and last bands.
  • Assembly steps place the bands from the bottom up, and the printable assembly guide shows the slice depth (or layer count) in place of a material thickness.

docs.title: Contributing and licence
docs.text: Refab Artist is free and open source. The code and the guide live in the GitHub repository. Contributions are welcome: bug reports, test models, fixes, new ideas.

docs.title: Reporting problems and sharing models
docs.text: Open an issue on the repository. Say which mode you were using, what you expected, and what happened. If you can share the model, attach it; failures on real models are the most useful thing you can report.

docs.title: Contributing code and documents
docs.text:
CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to build and check a change. In short:

  • Work on a branch (feat/<name>, fix/<name>, docs/<name> or chore/<name>), open a draft pull request on your first push, and keep to one feature per pull request.
  • Start a construction mode from its spec in docs/specs/, and run the checks on your own machine; there is no cloud CI beyond the check that records your signature on the contributor agreement.
  • A mode is done when it passes the functional gate, which checks that the parts it exports can be cut.
  • Keep the project clean-room: never copy other software, its resources, help text or output files. Test models need a recorded source.

docs.title: Contributor agreement
docs.text: You sign the contributor agreement once, on your first pull request, by replying to the bot's comment. You keep your copyright. The agreement licenses your contribution to the project under GPL-3.0 and additionally grants the maintainer a licence to use it under other terms. Read the full text in CONTRIBUTING.md before you contribute.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: Copyright (C) 2026 Pete Katz. Refab Artist is released under the GNU General Public License, version 3; see LICENSE. You may use, study, share and change it under those terms.

docs.title: Third-party components
docs.text:
Refab Artist links two components it did not write, and each keeps its own licence, both compatible with GPL-3.0:

  • Manifold for 3D mesh operations (Apache-2.0).
  • Clipper2 for 2D polygon operations (Boost Software License 1.0).

The full list is in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text: The Mac app is written in SwiftUI, with RealityKit for the 3D view. The cut-sheet modes and 3D Slices are specified in docs/specs/ in the repository, one file per mode.

docs.title: Curve
docs.text:
Curve is a two-family interlocking mode whose second family follows a curve. The first family is a set of parallel slices (the first-axis ribs). The second is a set of vertical ribs standing along a curve you shape, each one perpendicular to it (the curve ribs). Half-lap slots join the two families where they cross.

The cut sheet: slice outlines and ribs for an organic blob.

Slices crossed by curved ribs, in place.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Your model bends or sweeps: a tail, a handle, a wave, a figure with a lean.
  • You want the cross-ribs to fan out where the shape curves, so the structure follows the form instead of a straight grid.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• 1st Axis: the axis of the first family.
  • 1st Axis slices: how many first-axis ribs you want (1 to 72). The mode cuts fewer when that many would not fit with a web of material at least as thick as the stock left between slots. A note in orange under the control tells you when that happens and why.
  • Curve slices: how many curve ribs you want (2 to 72), with the same behaviour.
  • Amplitude: how far the default curve bows, in mm (10 to start with), at most the model's extent along it.
  • Thickness and Slot Offset: set slot width. Turn on Notch width if you want to type a width directly; it replaces them.

Curve slots are cut square, and Curve cuts no relief, so Tool Dia. is not shown.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Parts are first_axis_NNN and curve_NNN in the exports; each is a labelled cut-sheet part.
  • Assembly steps place the first-axis ribs, then insert the curve ribs.
  • Parts the joints hold together but not to the rest of the model are shown in blue on the cut sheet, meaning glue them in place.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• If a note says a first-axis rib has been "set off the even spacing", the mode moved it so the joints hold parts that would otherwise be joined only to each other. This is expected.
  • Where the curve bends sharply, the curve ribs stop short of the concave side, so that side is held by the first-axis ribs alone.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• On some organic models with the first axis set to Y and 5 mm stock, a few parts are marked to be glued in place instead of being held by joints. Another first axis, fewer curve slices or thinner stock join them.
  • A first-axis rib moved to join parts can leave a small lip near flat faces.

docs.title: Cutting and fit
docs.text: Refab Artist's checks show that an exported file is consistent and cuttable: every part fits its sheet, parts do not overlap, every cut is a closed shape, and slots are as wide as the stock. They cannot show that your parts fit your material. Kerf (the width of material your cutter removes), real stock thickness and the machine all matter, and no physical cut test has been recorded for 0.1.0. So cut a small test piece first.

docs.title: Kerf and Slot Offset
docs.text:
A slot is cut thickness + Slot Offset wide. Slot Offset is the extra width that makes the slot fit a piece of your stock after the cutter's own kerf is taken into account. Refab Artist applies it once, to the slots; do not also add kerf compensation in your cutter's software for the first run.

  • Too loose: lower Slot Offset.
  • Won't go together, or cracks the stock: raise it.
  • Interlocked and Curve: if you type a Notch width, it replaces thickness plus offset, and Slot Offset is not used.
  • Router cutters: a round bit cannot cut a square inside corner. Set Tool Dia. and a relief type (Interlocked Slot relief, Radial Relief Type) so the corners are cleared.

The material presets set a starting Slot Offset: Cardboard 3 mm 0.15 mm, Plywood 3 mm 0.10 mm, Plywood 6 mm 0.15 mm and Acrylic 3 mm 0.20 mm. They are starting points, not promises. The presets for standard sheet sizes use 0.254 mm (0.01 in).

docs.title: Measure your stock
docs.text: Use calipers, not the label. Plywood sold as "3 mm" is often a little more or less. Measure at several places, and put the real figure in Thickness. If your stock matches no preset, pick the nearest one and edit Thickness; the label switches to Custom. You can save the result with Save Current as Material... so it is a pick next time.

docs.title: A test cut
docs.text:
Do this once for each material and machine:

  1. Pick a small, quick model. A 50 mm cube in Interlocked works well: it makes real slots, and it is small enough for a quick, low-risk job.
  2. Set the material to your stock, using the measured thickness. Start with the preset's Slot Offset (for example 0.10 mm for 3 mm plywood).
  3. Export as DXF, SVG or PDF and import into your cutter software at 1:1 scale. Do not resize the drawing, and add no further kerf compensation.
  4. Cut the whole piece from one sheet. Keep every part, even ones that cut badly, until you have finished.
  5. Before assembly, measure the sheet thickness again and measure at least three slots on different parts.
  6. Dry-fit the parts by hand. Note the fit: too loose, hand-fit, tight, or impossible. Note any cracking, delamination, parts that needed sanding, or slots that look wrong, and which part or slot is worst.
  7. Adjust one thing at a time, usually Slot Offset, and cut again.

The fit is right when the piece goes together by hand without cracking, holds its shape under light handling, and needs no sanding or cleanup of the slots.

Keep notes

Write down your machine, power, speed, passes and the Slot Offset that worked. Save it as a material in Refab Artist and you will not need to do this again.

docs.title: Other things to check
docs.text:
• Scale: measure a finished part against the drawing. If it is off, the file was imported at the wrong scale or the model's size was wrong. See Getting started.
  • Grain and strength: thin necks between slots are weak. Curve cuts no more ribs than leave a web at least as thick as the stock between two slots, but wood grain and brittle materials can still break, so handle thin parts gently.
  • Folded needs stock that bends at the creases.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text: Once a model is sliced, File > Export Current Output... writes the file. Which formats are on offer depends on the mode.

docs.title: Cut sheets (flat-part modes)
docs.text:
Stacked, Interlocked, Radial, Curve and Folded write cut sheets. Every format is in millimetres. (Inflatables, the experimental mode, writes DXF, SVG and PDF.)

Format Use it for DXF Most laser and CNC software. Each part is on its own layer (where a part has scored guides they go on a layer of their own), and each sheet has an outline layer. SVG Vector editors and many laser programs. One file, with the sheets stacked down the page. PDF Viewing, printing, and editors such as Illustrator. One page per sheet, page size equal to the sheet. EPS Older workflows. One file per sheet, in a ZIP when there is more than one sheet.

Colour carries meaning in SVG and PDF cut sheets (and in EPS for Interlocked, Curve and Folded): blue lines are cuts, red lines are scored guides and labels. Line width is 0.1 mm. In Folded, fold lines are red when scored and blue when perforated, since the perforation is cut.

The labels are the part numbers shown in the app, and they match the assembly steps.

Use SVG, PDF or DXF to cut

For Stacked and Radial, the EPS writer lays the parts out in rows with its own numbering, and is vertically mirrored compared with the SVG and PDF. It is fine for a quick look but use SVG, PDF or DXF to cut.

docs.title: Sheet layout
docs.text: Parts are packed onto sheets of the size you set in Manufacturing Settings (Sheet W and Sheet H), with a Margin round each sheet and a Spacing gap between parts (10 mm each by default; the Export layout section has the same Margin and Spacing). Their order on a sheet carries no meaning. A part larger than the sheet is flagged and placed on its own sheet.

docs.title: Opening the file in your cutter's software
docs.text:
• Import at 1:1 scale. Do not resize the drawing.
  • Do not add extra kerf compensation for the first run; Slot Offset in Refab Artist already allows for it.
  • Map blue to cut and red to score or engrave.

docs.title: Parts as meshes (STL and OBJ)
docs.text:
Every mode can write its parts as a mesh.

  • STL is plain-text (ASCII): one solid holding every part.
  • OBJ has one named object per part (slice_001, primary_003, and so on) and notes its units as millimetres.

For the flat-part modes, the mesh is a way to check the assembly: each cut part extruded to its thickness and put back in place, so you can inspect the finished model in a 3D viewer before you cut. 3D Slices, Structures, Partition and MotherMold write meshes as their real output.

Under a tilted Slice Direction the mesh is written in the tilted frame, so the whole assembly comes out turned by the tilt. The 3D view and the cut sheets are not affected.

Partition and MotherMold can also package their pieces as a ZIP of separate files, a single OBJ with named parts, or all the parts laid out on one plate, and write an assembly map.

docs.title: Assembly guide
docs.text: File > Export Assembly Guide... writes a printable text guide: the model, the mode, your material settings, and every assembly step. It is the thing to have next to you while you build.

docs.title: Print
docs.text: File > Print... sends the cut sheets to a printer, which is handy for paper templates or hand cutting. It is available once a cut sheet is ready.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: File > Save Project... writes a .refabartist file with the model and every setting. File > Open Project... reads it back. Projects are for you to resume work or share a setup; they are not a cutting format.

docs.title: Headless export
docs.text: The same app can export without opening a window, from Terminal, for scripts and batch jobs. The README shows an example, and docs/development.md in the repository lists the modes and options. The app opens its window when run without those options.

docs.title: Folded
docs.text:
Folded does not slice. It treats the model's surface as a set of flat panels, unfolds them into one or more flat nets hinged along fold lines, and adds tabs, slots and other joinery to the edges that have to be joined again. Cut a net out, fold it along its fold lines and join the cut edges, and the model rebuilds as a shell.

The cut sheet for a low-poly head. Dashed lines are folds.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You want a hollow, lightweight paper-craft style model from card or thin sheet.
  • Your model is faceted (low-poly) or can be simplified to a modest number of faces.

Folded assumes your stock bends at the fold lines: card, thin sheet, or a perforated or kerf-cut crease. In stiff stock the fold lines must be cut through and the panels glued.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Joint Type: the joinery on the cut edges. The choices are None, Diamond, Gear, Laced, Multitab, Puzzle, Rivet, Tab, Ticked and Tongue, and Diamond is the starting choice. Choosing one loads sensible defaults for its size and spacing, and shows that joint's own size and spacing controls. Laced and Ticked fit nothing into a slot, and None cuts no slots, so Slot Offset is greyed out for those.
  • Detail (12 to 2000 faces, default 250), in the Simplify Form group: the polygon budget. Models with more faces are simplified to this number first, so every remaining face becomes a panel. Lower Detail gives fewer, bigger panels and an easier build. Vertex Count and Face Count beside it show the same budget.
  • Perforate: on by default; draws fold lines as perforation dashes (cut) instead of scored lines.
  • Split Panels: makes the nets smaller so they fit a smaller sheet. Disabled when every net already fits in half a sheet.
  • Edit seams: under Add/Remove Seams. While it is on, click a panel edge in the 3D view to force a cut there rather than a fold. Seams counts them and Clear removes them all.
  • Thickness and Slot Offset: the stock, and the clearance added to every slot a tab passes through.

Folded has no Slice Direction. Dense meshes are not refused; Folded builds a simplified shape around the object and lays that out.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Each net is one cut-sheet part. Fold lines are on their own layer (red when scored, blue when perforated).
  • Assembly steps are "Fold folded_panel_NNN", one per panel.
  • The mode tells you when some panels are left out or cut back because their neighbours' stock already occupies their space, for example "3 of 172 panels are left out". Thinner stock or a lower Detail keeps more of them.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start with a low Detail (the default is a good start) and a thin stock.
  • On curved models most edges are left plain to glue or tape.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Assembly step numbers count panels, while the cut sheet has one part per net, so step numbers differ from the sheet labels.
  • The STL and OBJ export of the cut parts lays them flat at their unfolded positions rather than folded into place.
  • The order in which parts can be assembled is not checked for Folded or Curve: a joint is checked where the parts end up, not that every part can be slid in turn.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page walks through one job from a model to a cut file. The same flow applies to every mode; the mode pages say what changes.

docs.title: 1. Open a model
docs.text:
Choose File > Import Model... (or Load Sample Model to try the app first). Refab Artist reads STL and OBJ files. The open dialog has an Up axis menu (Y, Z or X): choose the axis your file treats as up, so the model stands the right way round. Many modelling programs use Y.

The model appears in the 3D view and nothing is sliced yet. Loading happens in the background, so a large scan will not freeze the window.

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom. The view cube and the toolbar on the side of the view give you orbit, pan, zoom and fit.

docs.title: 2. Check the size
docs.text:
STL and OBJ files carry no units, so Refab Artist guesses from the model's size and shows its guess (mm, cm, m or inches) in the Object tab of the right inspector, under Object Size. If the model is the wrong size, change the unit, or type the real height, width or length. Uniform Scale is on by default, so the other two follow. Reset Size puts it back.

The same panel has a rotate row for X, Y and Z. A rotation here is baked into the model before slicing, so use it to stand the model up the way you want it built.

Tip

Everything downstream is in real units, so this is the step that decides whether your parts come out at the size you expect. Check it before you slice.

docs.title: 3. Pick a construction technique
docs.text:
Under Construction Technique in the left rail, choose how the model should be built:

If you want... Choose Layers you glue up in a stack Stacked A grid of slotted planks that slide together Interlocked Rings and fins around a centre Radial Slices with ribs along a curve Curve A folded shell from card or thin sheet Folded A layered mesh to 3D print 3D Slices Lattices, supports or a skin to print Structures A model split to fit your printer Partition A casting mold MotherMold

Nothing is sliced until you have chosen a technique. Choosing one reveals the sections below it.

docs.title: 4. Set your material
docs.text:
Manufacturing Settings describe the sheet you are cutting from:

  • Material: a preset (Cardboard 3 mm, Plywood 3 mm, Plywood 6 mm, Acrylic 3 mm), a standard sheet size (A4, Letter, B-series and P-series sizes, and so on), or a material you saved yourself. Picking one fills in thickness and slot offset; the sheet-size presets also fill in the sheet size and margin, and set the thickness to about 4.5 mm, so check Thickness after choosing one. If you then edit a value, the label switches to Custom; the preset itself is not changed.
  • Thickness: the real thickness of your stock. Measure it with calipers. Slice spacing and slot widths come from it.
  • Slot Offset: extra width added to every slot so parts fit after your cutter removes its kerf. The presets give a starting point; you will tune it with a test cut (see Cutting and fit).
  • Tool Dia.: the diameter of a router bit, used for the relief cut in the inside corners of slots (Interlocked and Radial). Leave it at 0 for a laser. It is greyed out while the mode's relief is off (Interlocked Slot relief off, Radial Relief Type Square).
  • Sheet W, Sheet H and Margin: the size of one sheet of your stock and the blank border kept round its edge. Parts are packed onto sheets of this size. The starting sheet is 600 by 300 mm with a 10 mm margin.

Values are stored in millimetres. The Units switch (mm or in) changes only what you see and type.

A row that the chosen technique never uses is left out, and one that another setting overrides is greyed out with a short note saying why. 3D Slices builds a layered mesh, so it has no Manufacturing Settings at all.

docs.title: 5. Set the technique's own settings
docs.text:
Technique Settings hold the controls specific to the mode: how many slices, which axis, relief type, joint type and so on. Each mode page lists the ones that matter.

Slice Direction is its own section below Technique Settings. It tilts the direction the model is cut along: it aims the cut and does not turn the model. Folded has no Slice Direction.

docs.title: 6. Slice
docs.text: Press Slice (or Generate, for the modes that build a mesh). Changing a setting does not recompute anything until you press it again, so you can set several things and slice once. The button reads Re-slice afterwards.

docs.title: 7. Check the cut-sheet preview
docs.text:
When slicing finishes you will see the 3D view with the parts in place and the cut sheet showing how the parts are laid out. The header shows how many sheets and parts there are.

  • Blue outlines are cut edges.
  • Red lines are scored guides: where the next piece will sit.
  • Red numbers label each part, matching the assembly steps.
  • A part filled red has a problem (difficult or impossible to build); a part filled blue is a detached piece that would fall off. Look at the Issues tab.

Click a sheet to see it larger. Use the View menu to show the 3D view, the sheet, or both side by side.

docs.title: 8. Step through the assembly
docs.text: Once there are parts, the Assembly panel lists one step per part. The previous and next arrows walk through them: the current part is highlighted in the 3D view and outlined on the cut sheet, and parts still to come show as faint ghosts, so you can watch the model grow. Click a part on the sheet to jump to its step. The Assembly panel also has a button to clear the highlight and one to export the assembly guide.

docs.title: 9. Export
docs.text: Choose File > Export Current Output... for the cut sheets (DXF, SVG, PDF or EPS) or the parts as a mesh (STL or OBJ). The mesh modes (3D Slices, Structures, Partition and MotherMold) offer STL and OBJ only. Export Assembly Guide... writes a printable guide, and Print... sends the sheets to a printer. See Exporting for what each format is for.

docs.title: 10. Save your project
docs.text: File > Save Project... saves a .refabartist file holding the model and every setting, so you can come back and change the material or the slice count later. Open Project... brings it back.

docs.title: Before you cut
docs.text: Do a test cut. Cut a small piece in your own stock, check the joints and adjust Slot Offset. Cutting and fit has the steps, and Safety covers the machine.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Assembly guide. A printable list of every assembly step, with the model, mode and material settings. See Exporting.

Cut sheet. The layout of all the flat parts on sheets of your stock, ready to export.

Dog-bone relief. A round cut-out at the inside corner of a slot so a round router bit can reach the corner and a square part can seat into it. Set with Tool Dia. and a relief type.

Dowel. A rod threaded through holes in every layer of a Stacked model to keep the layers lined up.

Fin. One of the vertical parts fanned around the centre in Radial.

First-axis rib. One of the parallel slices in Curve.

Fold line. A line on a Folded net where the stock bends. Drawn as a score or as perforation dashes.

Half-lap joint. A joint where each of two parts has a slot cut halfway through, so they cross flush. Used in Interlocked, Radial and Curve.

Kerf. The width of material a cutter removes. See Cutting and fit.

Mode. A construction technique: Stacked, Interlocked, Radial, Curve, Folded, 3D Slices, Structures, Partition, MotherMold or Inflatables.

Net. A group of panels laid flat in one piece, joined along fold lines, in Folded.

Notch. A cut into the edge of a part where another part slots in.

Object Size. The panel in the Object tab for checking and changing the units and size of the model.

Panel. A flat face of the model, made of triangles in one plane, in Folded.

Perforate. Draws Folded fold lines as cut dashes so thick stock folds easily.

Relief. See dog-bone relief.

Ring. One of the stacked cross-sections in Radial.

Seam. A place where two cut edges meet and are joined. In Partition, a place where two pieces meet and carry keys.

Slice. To compute the parts for the chosen mode. Also one layer of the model.

Slice Direction. The tilt of the cut away from the model's axes. It aims the cut; it does not turn the model.

Slot Offset. Extra width added to every slot so parts fit after the kerf. See Cutting and fit.

Stock. The sheet material you are cutting from.

Tool Dia. The diameter of the router bit used for relief cuts.

Watertight. A mesh with no holes: a closed surface. See Model repair.

docs.title: Inflatables (experimental)
docs.text:
Experimental

Inflatables is still in development. It may not produce usable parts, and you should not rely on it for a real project. It is hidden until you switch it on.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text: Open Settings (Refab Artist > Settings..., or Command-comma) and switch on Show experimental modes. Inflatables then appears in the Construction Technique list. Turning the switch off hides it again; a project that was saved in Inflatables keeps it until you choose another technique.

docs.title: What it tries to do
docs.text:
Inflatables plans flat panels and seams for an inflatable sculpture. It writes the panels as cut sheets (DXF, SVG or PDF), and the inflated shape as STL or OBJ.

A flat, sealed shape that does not stretch does not inflate into the shape you drew. It swells and pulls in, like a foil balloon, and any dent in the model tends to pop outward unless something inside holds it. Treat the output as a first-pass pattern and a way to see where the requested shape cannot be reached, not as a finished design.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use it to explore. Cut a small test panel in cheap material before committing to anything.
  • Because the mode is experimental, it is not covered by the cuttability gate the supported modes pass; see the Troubleshooting page for the status of each mode.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
  • macOS 15 (Sequoia) or newer. Version 0.1.0 was built and checked on macOS 26 only; it has not been run on macOS 15 or 14, so tell us if you hit trouble there.

Refab Artist needs no account and no internet connection once it is installed.

docs.title: Download the app
docs.text:
1. Go to the Releases page and download Refab-Artist-0.1.0.zip.
  2. Double-click the zip. Refab Artist appears next to it.
  3. Drag Refab Artist into your Applications folder.
  4. Open it.

The app is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, with the ticket stapled, so macOS opens it like any other app without warnings or extra steps.

The app does not update itself. To update, download the new version from the Releases page and drag it over the old one. Your saved projects stay where you saved them.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
You need a Mac with Apple silicon, macOS 15 or newer, and Xcode (or its command line tools) with Swift 6. Manifold and Clipper2 are vendored as prebuilt static libraries, so nothing else needs installing.

git clone https://github.com/peterkatz/refab-artist.git
cd refab-artist

# Build an app you can double-click (a release build; the first one takes a few minutes):
tools/package_app.sh
open "build/Refab Artist.app"

tools/package_app.sh builds in release configuration and writes build/Refab Artist.app, signed ad hoc so it runs on your Mac. To build or run without packaging:

swift build --package-path app/RefabArtist -c release
swift run --package-path app/RefabArtist RefabArtist

docs.title: Optional: a 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse
docs.text: If you have a 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse and 3Dconnexion's driver is installed, Refab Artist can use it to move around the 3D view. The app loads the driver library at run time, and the download is signed in a way that allows that. Nothing needs setting up in Refab Artist; if the driver is not installed, the app works as normal with the mouse and trackpad.

docs.title: What is in the window
docs.text:
The window is organised around one flow, left to right:

  • Left rail: the whole build, top to bottom: your model, the construction technique, manufacturing settings, technique settings, slice direction, and the Slice button, followed by Assembly and Export once there are parts.
  • Centre: the 3D view, and the cut-sheet preview once you have sliced.
  • Right inspector: tabs for Object (size and Modify Form), Viewport (how the model looks), Issues and Stats.

Getting started walks through it with a model.

Try it without a model

File > Load Sample Model opens a built-in sample cube so you can look around before you bring your own.

docs.title: Interlocked
docs.text:
Interlocked cuts the model with two families of slices at right angles and carves a half-lap slot wherever they cross. The parts slide together into a grid, so you can build the model without glue.

The cut sheet: slotted planks for a small chair.

The two families in place.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You want a light, open "waffle" structure that holds together by its joints.
  • Your model is reasonably compact. The grid works best on shapes you can imagine cut into planks.
  • You have a laser or CNC router. Slot fit matters here, so plan a test cut.

docs.title: How the slices run
docs.text: Both families are vertical planks laid across the model's longest side, so the longest axis is never a slicing direction. For a model that is clearly taller than it is wide, the planks run on X and Y; for one clearly longer in X, on Y and Z; and so on. The Primary and Secondary axis pickers only apply when all three sides are about equal (a cube or a sphere). Otherwise they are greyed out and the panel tells you which axes are in use.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Distribute count: turn it on to choose how many Slices per family (1 to 240). Without it there are 10 per family, spread evenly. The count, not the stock thickness, sets the spacing.
  • Thickness and Slot Offset (Manufacturing Settings): the slot is cut thickness + slot offset wide. This is the setting you tune with a test cut.
  • Notch width: turn it on and type a slot Width directly. It replaces thickness plus offset, and Slot Offset is greyed out.
  • Slot angle: flares the mouth of each slot (0 to 60 degrees) to make assembly easier.
  • Slot relief and Tool Dia.: turn on Slot relief to add a round dog-bone relief at the inside corners of each slot for a router bit. It is cut for the Tool Dia. in Manufacturing Settings, the bit's diameter; leave that at 0 for a laser.
  • Slice Direction: tilt the cut.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Each part is numbered with its family: Z-6, Y-2, or Y-2-1 when a slice falls into several pieces.
  • Assembly steps place all the primary parts first, then insert the secondary parts into their slots.
  • STL and OBJ exports let you check the assembled grid.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• If the planks are thick compared with the slice spacing, the slots can merge and each part loses its slotted half. Nothing warns you. Use Distribute count to space the slices further apart, or thinner stock.
  • Parts that fit loosely? Lower Slot Offset. Parts that will not go together? Raise it. Cutting and fit has a method.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Interlocked exports carry no part positions, so the project's own checks confirm the slots are the right width and cuttable but cannot confirm that every pair of slots mates. A test cut matters.
  • In the STL and OBJ export, slots are only cut into parts whose outline is a plain rectangle; other parts are exported without their slots.

docs.title: Model repair
docs.text:
Scans and downloaded models are often not quite solid: they have holes, flipped faces or stray pieces. The Modify Form tools in the Object tab of the right inspector work on the whole model before you slice, without changing the file you imported. You can remove a tool at any time to go back to the imported mesh.

There are three tools: Make Watertight, Hollow and Thicken. Each has an eye button to preview its result in the 3D view and an Apply button to use it. The slice, the cut sheets and the exports then use the modified model.

Closed, not perfect

"Watertight" here means closed: no holes. A healed organic scan can keep harmless self-contact edges, so the counts shown are real counts, not a promise of a perfect solid.

docs.title: Make Watertight
docs.text:
Closes a broken model. It begins by diagnosing the model: it measures the surface and marks each problem in the 3D view. Each opening is listed; click a row to see it in the view. There are three methods:

  • Fix in place repairs only the problem spots and caps each opening, leaving every other triangle exactly as it was. Use it for a model that is nearly solid. For each opening you can choose to Cap it or Leave open, and give the cap a dish or dome shape.
  • Make walls gives an open skin real walls. The outside stays exactly as modelled, the wall grows inward, and the rim stays open. Use it for a cup, a bowl or a vase that was modelled as a thin skin. You set the Wall thickness.
  • Rebuild as solid rebuilds the whole surface as one closed solid, filling cavities. Use it for scans too damaged for the other two. Detail controls how fine it is; higher is finer and slower. Because it re-meshes the surface, it changes every triangle.

Try them in that order: the first changes the least.

docs.title: Hollow
docs.text:
Turns a solid model into a shell with the wall thickness you choose (0.5 to 30 mm). The outside looks the same; the inside is hollow. Because the shell is interior, the solid 3D view looks unchanged. The slice contours show it, as rings on the cut sheet in Stacked, for example.

A 50 mm sphere hollowed with a 4 mm wall, sliced in Stacked: each layer is a ring.

Use Hollow to save material, or to build a model as a shell that is later filled.

docs.title: Thicken
docs.text: Grows every face outward by the amount you choose (0.1 to 20 mm). It rescues thin details that would not survive cutting.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Check Object Size first: a repair at the wrong scale uses the wrong wall thickness.
  • The Issues and Stats tabs show mesh health: open edges, non-manifold edges, degenerate faces and duplicates.
  • Make Watertight can run under Hollow or Thicken when the model needs closing first.

docs.title: MotherMold
docs.text:
MotherMold builds a 3D-printable casting mold around your model, in two or four keyed parts with a clamping rim to bolt them together, a pour hole and air vents. It writes meshes (STL or OBJ, or a ZIP or plate of them), not cut sheets.

A two-part rigid mold for a 50 mm sphere, laid out. One half has the pour funnel, the other the cavity. Both have the clamping rim with bolt holes.

docs.title: What are you making?
docs.text:
The panel opens with three goals. Pick one first:

  • Cast copies makes a rigid "mother mold" shell that holds poured silicone. You cast silicone around your master in the printed shell, then cast your final copies in the silicone. Silicone flexes off undercuts, so undercut detection is only informational here. This is the right choice for detailed sculpture and several copies.
  • Rigid mold makes a hard printed mold whose cavity matches your model, for casting directly into it. Because the printed mold cannot flex, undercuts matter: the app checks that every part can be pulled away cleanly, and blocks export if it cannot prove it. It suits simple shapes and materials that release easily.
  • Production tooling is for repeated production runs. It adds sections for the printed master and how it is held, and exports one manufacturing ZIP with the parts and their documents. Treat it as the most advanced choice.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Parts (under Split): 2-part or 4-part. A four-part mold is cut by two planes.
  • Mode: Auto or Manual parting. With Manual you choose each plane's Axis (X, Y or Z) and Offset. Auto uses two orthogonal planes for a four-part mold.
  • Wall under Shell: the thickness of the mold wall. For Cast copies there are also Silicone thickness and Detail softening, which together set the Total cavity offset shown beneath them.
  • Flat floor and Floor: a closed flat base, and its thickness.
  • Keys & clamping (a folded section): Type of registration key (None, Tapered round or Tapered bar), with its size, Depth, Fit clearance and Keys per seam. The keys have a release taper so the parts separate easily, and the female pocket is sized with the clearance. Below them, Clamping rim adds a flange plate at the parts' meeting faces, with its Width, Thick, number of Bolt holes and Bolt Ø.
  • Pour & vents (a folded section): Pour hole mode (Auto or Manual), Pour hole Ø, the number of Vents and Vent Ø.
  • Output (a folded section): Package (for example separate STLs in a zip, a combined OBJ, or a single laid-out plate) and Assembly guide.

Press Build mold when you are ready. Nothing is built while you change settings.

The master model must be watertight (a closed shape). If it is not, the build tells you in plain words and points you at Make Watertight before you go further.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Each mold part is checked to be a watertight, finite mesh.
  • An assembly guide lists the parts, parting planes and steps: clean the casting faces, align and key the parts, clamp them with bolts, pour slowly through the funnel, let air out through every vent, cure, and open the mold. For Cast copies it begins with how the master is held while you pour.
  • Explode in the 3D view pulls the parts apart so you can inspect the inside. Pressing it again restores the assembled view. Undercut markers can be switched on to show where the model would catch.
  • Export is blocked if a requirement is not met, for example if the clamping rim does not cover every interface or a key is damaged, and the panel says why. The parts stay available for inspection.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• With silicone, a printed fit is not a liquid seal. Seal the master's locating land with clay or a compatible sealant before you pour.
  • Check bed fit and supports in your own printer software; MotherMold verifies the mold geometry, not your print.
  • A small mold may not fit the default 12 mm pour funnel. Choose a smaller Pour hole Ø.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
Some combinations are known not to build in 0.1.0; see Troubleshooting:

  • a four-part reusable silicone mold on some models (a head-shaped test model stops while placing the liner registration buttons),
  • a four-part mold of a scanned hand with X and Z planes through its centre,
  • the funnel and a very small mold.

docs.title: Partition
docs.text:
Partition splits a model into watertight pieces. In Fit Printer it also adds locating keys at every seam, so the printed pieces line up when you glue them. It exports meshes (STL or OBJ), not cut sheets.

An organic blob split to fit a 60 mm build volume, shown laid out. The pins on the cut face fit sockets in the next piece.

docs.title: Two purposes
docs.text: A Purpose picker at the top of the panel chooses what Partition is for.

docs.title: Fit Printer
docs.text:
Use this when the model is bigger than your printer.

  1. Pick a Printer preset from the list (Bambu Lab X1C, A1 and A1 mini, Prusa MK4, Creality Ender-3 and others), or choose Custom and enter a build volume (W, D and H).
  2. Set the Bed margin, the space to keep clear at the edge of the bed.
  3. Under Splitting, choose Auto-fit or Manual. Auto-fit works out the cuts that make every piece fit, and offers a Strategy: fewest parts, or even part sizes. Manual lets you add cut planes (Add X, Add Y, Add Z) and move and angle them in the 3D view yourself. From Auto-fit seeds the planes from the automatic result, so you can auto-fit first and then adjust by hand.
  4. Under Seams & keys, choose a Key: locating pins (pin and socket), a rectangular wedge key, or none for a plain butt joint. The key size, length and tolerance are adjustable.
  5. Press Generate. Splitting a dense model takes a moment and runs in the background. A Fit check shows how many pieces there are and whether they all fit.

docs.title: Split by Undercuts
docs.text:
Use this to make pieces that can be moulded: it divides a watertight model into a small number of pieces that can each be pulled free of a mold. You set the Undercut tolerance, the Pull policy (Automatic, or Fixed to a direction you choose), the Max pieces, and a Priority (Fewer pieces, Balanced or Cleaner seams). A Search quality setting (Quick, Standard or Thorough) is under the advanced settings. Planning can run for a while, and you can cancel it; pieces from the previous run are kept.

Check scanned models yourself

The undercut measurement is tested on simple shapes and on scans, and the split itself is tested on simple shapes. The tests that split a scanned hand and an open mask do not run yet. On an organic scan, inspect every piece in the 3D view before you make a mold from it. Fit Printer is not affected.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Partition writes:

Fit Printer offers three Packaging choices:

  • Separate files in a .zip, one STL per piece;
  • One file, named parts: a single OBJ with a named object per piece;
  • Laid out on one plate: all the pieces placed on a single plate.

Naming chooses grid labels (A1, B2...) or sequential names (part-01...). Include assembly map adds a map saying which piece joins which. Split by Undercuts exports as STL or OBJ from the Export section.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Make the model watertight first if it is a scan; see Model repair.
  • Pieces stay solid. Partition does not hollow or thicken them.
  • Pieces are checked as watertight meshes. Printer settings (supports, temperatures, speeds) stay with your slicing software.

docs.title: Radial
docs.text:
Radial builds the model from rings and fins. The rings are a stack of cross-sections along the vertical axis. The fins are vertical sections fanned around the model's centre like the segments of an orange. Wherever a ring and a fin cross there is a half-lap joint, a notch in the ring and a slot in the fin, so the two families lock together.

The cut sheet: notched rings and fins for a torus.

The rings and fins in place.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Your model is round or roughly turned: a vase, a bust, a helmet, a lamp shade.
  • You want the structure to read as rings at every height, with fins giving it stiffness.

Rings are always cut across the vertical (Z) axis, whatever the model's proportions, so stand the model up first.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Method: By Count or By Distance, with the matching 1st Axis value: the number of rings (1 to 72, 10 to start with), or the spacing between them in mm. Rings are never closer than one stock thickness, so you may get fewer than you asked for.
  • Radial (Count): how many fins, 1 to 72 (6 to start with).
  • Thickness and Slot Offset: set the width of every notch and slot.
  • Relief Type: Square, Horizontal, Vertical or Dog Bone. Relief rounds out the inside corner of each notch so a router bit can reach it. It is cut for Tool Dia. in Manufacturing Settings, which is greyed out for Square relief because square cuts no circles.
  • Notch Angle is shown but disabled: radial notches are always cut square.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Parts are numbered first_axis_NNN for rings and radial_NNN for fins in the exports.
  • Assembly steps place the rings from the bottom up, then insert the fins.
  • A ring piece that no fin reaches is left out, and the notes name it.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Asking for 8 fins currently gives 10. See Troubleshooting.
  • Pieces that meet the other family only where a line crosses the model more than once are marked to be glued, not locked.
  • Use dog-bone relief with a CNC router; a laser does not need it.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: A cut file moves a real machine, and a laser or a router can hurt you or start a fire. This page is general good practice, not legal or professional advice. Your machine's manual, your makerspace's rules and the safety data for your materials come first.

docs.title: What Refab Artist checks, and what it doesn't
docs.text: Before a file reaches you, Refab Artist checks that it is consistent and cuttable: parts fit the sheet, cuts are closed shapes, slots are the right width. That is not the same as safe. It cannot see your machine, your material, your settings, the space around you or where the emergency stop is. Those are yours.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Never cut PVC, vinyl or unknown plastics

Cutting PVC (polyvinyl chloride), vinyl, and many coated or imitation-leather materials with a laser releases chlorine gas and hydrochloric acid, which are toxic and destroy the machine. If you do not know exactly what a material is, do not cut it. Check its label or ask the supplier for the safety data sheet.

  • Use materials sold for your kind of machine. Plywood, MDF, solid wood, cardboard and cast acrylic are common for laser cutting; check that the glue in plywood and MDF is one your machine and extraction can handle.
  • Some plastics, such as polycarbonate and some foams, burn badly or give off harmful fumes. Leave them alone unless your machine's maker says they are safe.
  • Cutting produces fine dust and fumes, including from wood and MDF. Treat them as something to extract, not breathe.

docs.title: Laser cutters
docs.text:
• Ventilation and extraction. Run the extraction (or vent outdoors) every time, and keep the filters in good order.
  • Never leave a running laser. Stay with the machine until the job is done. Cutting wood, card and acrylic can ignite, and a small flame can become a fire in seconds.
  • Fire. Keep a suitable fire extinguisher within reach and know how to use it. Keep the bed and the area underneath clean, because offcuts and dust burn.
  • Eye protection. Keep the lid closed while the laser is on. If you must work with the lid open or the machine's guards removed, wear eyewear rated for your laser's wavelength; ordinary glasses and sunglasses are not enough.
  • Test your settings on scrap first, and use the lowest power and passes that cut cleanly.

docs.title: CNC routers
docs.text:
• Wear eye and ear protection, and a dust mask or use dust extraction.
  • Clamp the sheet down firmly. Keep hands, hair, sleeves and jewellery away from the spindle.
  • Know where the emergency stop is. Do not leave the machine running.
  • Use the right bit for the material and the right speeds and feeds for your machine.

docs.title: Cutting by hand
docs.text:
• Use a sharp blade and a steel ruler, cut away from your body, and use a cutting mat.
  • Cut in several shallow passes rather than one deep one.

docs.title: Before every job
docs.text:
• Check the file's scale and that you have chosen the right material.
  • Look the sheet over in the cut-sheet preview and read the Issues tab.
  • Run a small test first, as described in Cutting and fit.
  • Keep the emergency stop within reach, and stay with the machine.

docs.title: Stacked
docs.text:
Stacked cuts the model into parallel layers along one axis. Each layer becomes flat parts. Glue the parts up in order and the model rebuilds as a terraced solid. It is the simplest mode and the easiest place to start.

The cut sheet: a 50 mm sphere in 3 mm stock, 16 numbered layers.

The same layers in place.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• You want a solid-looking sculpture, a bust or a vase from sheet material and don't mind the stepped surface (or plan to sand it).
  • You want parts that need no slots or joinery, only glue.
  • A layer that falls into several separate pieces is fine: each piece becomes its own labelled part.

Choose Interlocked or Radial instead if you want a lighter, open structure that holds together without glue.

docs.title: Controls that matter
docs.text:
• Primary: the axis the layers are stacked along: X, Y or Z. The layers are drawn in the plane of the other two axes. Stand the model up first (in Object Size) if you want the layers to run a particular way.
  • Thickness (Manufacturing Settings): the real thickness of your stock. With automatic distribution it is also the spacing between layers.
  • Method: Automatic spaces the layers one thickness apart, centred on the model. By Count gives you exactly that many Slices (1 to 240); By Distance a Spacing you choose. Custom lets you place each layer yourself: turn on Edit Slices, click a layer in the 3D view and drag it along the axis, use the add and delete buttons, or press Distribute Evenly to start over.
  • Dowel holes (their own Dowels section, below Slice Direction): turn on to cut matching holes through every layer so a rod threads the stack and keeps it lined up while the glue dries. Choose the Shape (Square, Pencil, Round, Cross, Horizontal Slot or Vertical Slot), the Diameter and the Inset. The Automatic button stands rods where they pass through the most layers, and the number beside it says how many. Switch on Edit placement and click the sliced model to add a rod, drag one to move it through the whole stack, and press Delete to remove it.
  • Slice Direction: tilt the layers away from the axis.

Stacked does not use Slot Offset or Tool Dia., so those rows are not shown.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Every part is numbered. Digits 6 and 9 carry an underline so you can tell them apart when a part is turned.
  • Red scored guide lines inside each part show where the next layer sits, so you can line it up while gluing.
  • The assembly steps are one per layer, in order: "Place slice_001", then 002, and so on.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Thinner stock gives a smoother surface and more parts. Check the part count before you commit to a big job.
  • Use dowels on anything taller than a handful of layers. Without them the stack can drift.
  • The STL and OBJ export shows the assembled result, so you can check the look in another viewer before cutting.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• When dowels are switched off, a layer with a hole in it exports to STL/OBJ with the hole filled. Turn dowels on, or treat the mesh as a rough preview.
  • The EPS export for Stacked lays the parts out in rows and is drawn mirrored top-to-bottom compared with the SVG and PDF; use SVG, PDF or DXF for cutting. See Exporting.

docs.title: Structures
docs.text:
Structures builds lattice-like geometry from a model, as a printable mesh (STL or OBJ). It has three types, chosen with the Type picker: Infill, Supports and Skin.

Skin: the surface of an organic blob replaced by a network of struts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Structures has its own Generate button (it reads Re-generate afterwards). Nothing is recomputed while you move sliders; press it when you are ready. The work runs in the background, and the 3D view shows exactly the geometry that will be exported. If you change a setting after generating, the old result is hidden until you generate again.

Structures, like the other mesh modes, has no cut sheet and no Manufacturing Settings.

docs.title: Infill
docs.text:
Fills the model with a pattern. There are patterns in four families:

  • Planar: Triangle, Grid, Tri-Hexagon, Cross, Concentric.
  • Lattice: Cubic, Octet, Quarter Cubic, Cubic Subdivision, Cross 3D.
  • TPMS (gyroid): Gyroid · Lofted, Gyroid · Marching Cubes, Gyroid · Network, and Graded Gyroid.
  • Op Art: Stanczak, Vasarely, Riley Movement-in-Squares, Graded Rings, Wave Grating.

The main controls are Cell (the cell size) and Wall (the wall thickness). For some patterns (for example Triangle, Grid, Cross, Graded Gyroid and Wave Grating) the cell size can also vary across the model: choose a Density source of Uniform, an Image (a grayscale picture projected onto the model), Attractors (cells shrink toward a point such as the centre, top or bottom) or Near Surface. Patterns that cannot follow a density source disable those controls and say why.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text:
Grows organic, tree-like supports. Pick the Mode:

  • Sculpture seeds branch tips densely on a Surface you choose (Up Facing by default, or Down Facing) so the branches build that surface up and can be used as a sculptural form in their own right.
  • Scaffold makes the classic printable supports: it finds overhangs (the Surface choice does not apply) and grows branches that avoid the model.

Tip spacing (Tip Gap), tip and branch diameters (Tip Dia, Branch) and branch angles are all adjustable.

docs.title: Skin
docs.text:
Replaces the model's surface with a hollow strut network, so the result is a standalone lattice object. Choose the Style and the Pattern (Voronoi, Hex or Triangles). Set the Cell size and the Strut diameter; Variation and Strut Var make the cells and struts more organic, and Clip chooses whether the struts sit inside the surface, outside it or straddle it. Cell size follows the same density sources as Infill.

Perforated is not available yet

The Style picker lists Struts and Perforated, but in version 0.1.0 only Struts generates. If you pick Perforated the panel says it is deferred.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Try a coarse cell size first. Fine cells on a large model make very large files.
  • If a result is coarsened to keep it manageable, the panel says so.
  • Check the result in your slicer before printing; Structures makes the geometry, not the printer settings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and known issues
docs.text: This page covers common problems and the known issues in version 0.1.0. The full list is in the release notes.

docs.title: Mode status
docs.text:
Mode Status Stacked Supported Interlocked Supported Radial Supported Curve Supported with known limits Folded Supported with known limits 3D Slices Supported Structures Supported Partition Supported with known limits MotherMold Supported with known limits Make Watertight, Hollow, Thicken Supported Inflatables Experimental

"Supported" means the mode passes the checks listed in the release notes. None of them has had a physical cut test yet; cut a small test piece in your own material first (Cutting and fit).

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
The model is tiny or huge. The file's units are guessed. Open the Object tab and set the unit or type the real size under Object Size.

Nothing happens after I pick a technique. Settings changes do not recompute anything. Press Slice (or Generate).

A control is greyed out. Another setting overrides it, and a short note under it says which. For example, Slot Offset is greyed out while Notch width is on.

The parts don't fit together. Adjust Slot Offset and cut again; see Cutting and fit.

Fewer parts than I asked for. Curve, Radial and Interlocked cut fewer ribs or rings when that many would stand closer than the stock thickness, or leave too little material between slots. A note under the control says so.

A part is red or blue on the cut sheet. Red means a part that is difficult or impossible to build; blue means a piece that would fall off and must be glued in place. Look at the Issues tab.

The model has holes or flipped faces. Use Make Watertight first.

The Inflatables mode is missing. It is experimental. Turn on Show experimental modes in Settings.

docs.title: Cut-sheet modes
docs.text:
• Curve, first axis Y, 5 mm stock. On some organic models a few parts are marked (blue on the cut sheet) to be glued in place instead of being held by joints. Another first axis, fewer curve slices or thinner stock join them.
  • Curve, ribs moved to join parts. A first-axis rib moved off its even spacing can leave a small lip near flat faces.
  • Slice Direction and STL / OBJ. With a tilted Slice Direction, the STL and OBJ files are written in the tilted frame: the whole assembly comes out turned by the tilt. The 3D view and the cut sheets are not affected.
  • Radial fin count. Asking for 8 fins gives 10.
  • Interlocked and the joint check. The project's checks confirm slot widths and cuttability on Interlocked but cannot check that every pair of slots mates.
  • Interlocked, thick stock on a small model. If the stock is as thick as the slice spacing, the slots merge and each part loses its slotted half. Nothing warns about it; set Distribute count to fix it.
  • Radial. Ring pieces that no fin reaches are left out, and the notes name them. Pieces that meet the other family only where a line crosses the model more than once are marked to be glued, not locked.
  • Curve. Where the curve bends sharply, the curve ribs stop short of the concave side. A few ribs have thin webs, and notes name them.
  • Folded. It assumes the stock bends at the fold lines. On curved models most edges are left plain to glue or tape. Assembly step numbers count panels, while the cut sheet has one part per net, so they differ from the sheet labels.
  • Assembly order is not checked for Curve and Folded.

docs.title: Partition
docs.text: • Split by Undercuts on scanned models is not checked yet. On an organic scan, check each piece in the 3D view before you mould it. Fit Printer is not affected.

docs.title: MotherMold
docs.text:
• Four-part reusable silicone mold on some models. On a low-poly head test model the build stops while placing the liner registration buttons. No mold package is written.
  • Four-part mold of a hand scan with X and Z planes through its centre. Two of the quarter shells come out in two pieces each, and the planner refuses a mold part in two pieces. The X/Y and Y/Z plane pairs on the same scan work.
  • Prepared master of an already healed hand scan. The prepared master can be refused.
  • Pour funnel on a small mold. The default 12 mm sealed pour funnel does not fit on one part of a 50 mm cube parted through its centre; a 10 mm one does. Choose a smaller spout on small molds.

docs.title: Other
docs.text:
• Physical cut tests are not done.
  • Inflatables is experimental.
  • The app has been run on macOS 26 only.
  • At small sizes, such as Finder's list view, macOS 26 shows the app icon on a light-grey backdrop.
  • No Intel, Windows or Linux build, no automatic update, no Homebrew cask and no Mac App Store release.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Open an issue on the GitHub repository. Say which mode you were in, what you expected and what happened, and attach the model if you can share it.
